600: I sell hats. Just hats. If you want gossip, that stall is two down and much cheaper.
601: I shout about hats all day. My voice is tired. The hats are fine.
602: People ask if the hats come with a story. No. They come with a brim.
603: I have forty hats and one customer. He is looking at the trinkets.
604: A good hawker sells you a hat you did not know you wanted. I am a good hawker.
605: I called out to a hundred people today. Two waved. One bought a hat.
606: My trinkets are shiny. My hats are practical. I recommend both, loudly.
607: I know every face on this street. I do not know their names. I know their hat size.
608: Someone asked me for a secret. I offered a hat instead. He took the hat.
609: I sell hats, not information. The hats are much better made.
610: By evening I have no voice left, so I sell the last few hats by pointing and looking hopeful.
611: I can spot a head that needs a hat from across the square. It is a quiet talent.
612: A trinket for luck, a hat for the sun. I do not sell luck, honestly.
613: I lowered my voice once, to rest it. Sold nothing. Back to shouting.
614: The best hat I own is on my own head. It is not for sale. Do not ask.
615: Children like the trinkets. Adults pretend not to. Then they buy two.
616: I have described this hat forty times today. It is still just a hat.
617: My stall is loud on purpose. A quiet hat seller is just a man standing near hats.
618: I do not pick my customers. The sun does. On a bright day, everyone suddenly needs a hat.
619: End of the day, I count the hats I have left. That tells me how loud to be tomorrow.
620: I could sell this at the asking price. But then what would we talk about?
621: Every coin matters to me. I once haggled over one for a full hour. I enjoyed it.
622: You offer half, I ask for double, we meet in the middle. That is friendship.
623: I do not lose sleep over the goods. I lose sleep over the last coin of a good haggle.
624: A customer paid my full price today without arguing. I felt cheated, somehow.
625: A quick sale leaves me restless. Make me fight for every coin, or I feel we skipped the good part.
626: My prices are firm. My prices are also flexible. It depends on how you ask.
627: I count my coins twice each night. Once for the total, once for the joy of it.
628: Everything on this stall has two prices. The one I say, and the one you earn.
629: You want a discount? Sit down. This will take a while, and I have tea.
630: I have argued over the price of a button. I regret nothing. I won the button.
631: A fair deal is one where we both walk away sure we cheated the other.
632: I never name my lowest price first. That would end the conversation too soon.
633: Some sell to be rich. I sell to argue. The coins are just how we keep score.
634: You will pay more than you wanted and less than I hoped. That is a good market.
635: I remember every haggle I have ever lost. There are two. I still think about them.
636: My grandmother taught me to haggle. She once argued with the tax man, and won.
637: The goods change every week. The bargaining does not. That is the real business.
638: I raised my price when you frowned, because a frown means you still want it.
639: Come back tomorrow and we will do this all again. I look forward to it, truly.
